body.back: The mechanisms keeping plasma H+ constant: pH = −log[H+], normal 7.37 to 7.43, despite a daily acid load mostly from protein metabolism. Regulated by buffers, the lungs and the kidneys.

Volatile: CO2, a weak acid, eliminated quickly by the lungs via carbonic anhydrase. Fixed: lower amounts but strongly dissociated; organic (lactic acid, ketones) and mineral (phosphoric, sulphuric); eliminated by the kidneys as free H+ (for bicarbonate reabsorption) and bound H+ (NH4+, NaH2PO4).
Acid-base pairs neutralising excess or deficit of H+. Henderson-Hasselbalch: pH = pKa + log [A-]/[AH]. Capacity is higher when pKa is near pH and concentration is high.

The main extracellular buffer: immediate first line of defence, limited by consumption of bicarbonate. Most effective because of high concentration, pKa near body pH, and dual lung and kidney regulation. pH = 6.1 + log [HCO3-] / (0.03 x PCO2).

Extracellular: proteinate (low capacity), phosphate NaH2PO4/Na2HPO4 (low capacity, important in urine). Intracellular: haemoglobin (high capacity; HbO2 releases O2 and binds H+ in tissues, releases H+ in lungs), proteins, bone phosphates and carbamates (important in acidosis).

title: How do the lungs regulate pH?
subject: subj:biochem

body.front: How do the lungs regulate pH?
body.back: Fast control of PCO2 by pH-sensitive medullary centres. Metabolic acidosis: hyperventilation lowers PaCO2. Metabolic alkalosis: hypoventilation raises PaCO2. Limited in capacity.

title: How do the kidneys regulate pH?
subject: subj:biochem

body.front: How do the kidneys regulate pH?
body.back: Slow but powerful and lasting. Reabsorb filtered bicarbonate proximally (excrete it above 28 mmol/L). Excrete H+: free (sets urine pH, down to 4.4; H+/Na+ and H+/K+ exchange, so acidosis causes hyperkalaemia), titratable acid (one third, H2PO4-), ammonium (two thirds, stimulated by acidosis and hyperkalaemia). Each H+ excreted regenerates one HCO3-.

title: How are blood gases sampled and read?
subject: subj:biochem

body.front: How are blood gases sampled and read?
body.back: Arterial puncture (radial, femoral) or capillary in newborns; heparinised airtight syringe, anaerobic, on ice, within 1 hour; correct for temperature. pH 7.37 to 7.43, PaCO2 37 to 43 mmHg, PaO2 75 to 100 mmHg, HCO3- 22 to 26 mmol/L, SaO2 95 to 99 percent, anion gap 12 ± 2, lactate 1 to 2 mmol/L. Venous bicarbonate on heparin, not EDTA.

Metabolic acidosis: pH under 7.38, HCO3- under 22, PaCO2 falls. Respiratory acidosis: pH under 7.38, PaCO2 over 42, HCO3- rises. Metabolic alkalosis: pH over 7.42, HCO3- over 26, PaCO2 rises. Respiratory alkalosis: pH over 7.42, PaCO2 under 36, HCO3- falls. Mixed: both change in the same harmful direction.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biochem

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Buffer systems. Bicarbonate/carbonic acid is the main extracellular buffer; haemoglobin the main red-cell buffer.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biochem

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Kidneys. Reabsorb filtered bicarbonate, excrete H⁺ as titratable acid and ammonium, regenerate bicarbonate.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biochem

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Lungs. Chemoreceptors change ventilation to eliminate or retain CO₂ within minutes.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biochem

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Metabolic acidosis. pH < 7.38, HCO₃⁻ < 22 mmol/L, compensated by hyperventilation.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biochem

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Metabolic alkalosis. pH > 7.42, HCO₃⁻ > 26 mmol/L, compensated by hypoventilation.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biochem

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Respiratory acidosis. pH < 7.38, PaCO₂ > 42 mmHg, compensated by renal HCO₃⁻ retention.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biochem

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Respiratory alkalosis. pH > 7.42, PaCO₂ < 36 mmHg, compensated by lower HCO₃⁻.

title: What regulates acid-base balance, in order?
subject: subj:biochem

body.front: What regulates acid-base balance, in order?
body.back: Buffers (immediate), lungs (minutes, PaCO₂), kidneys (hours to days, HCO₃⁻ and H⁺).
Volatile: CO₂, eliminated by the lungs via carbonic anhydrase. Fixed: organic (lactate, ketones) and mineral (phosphoric, sulphuric), eliminated by the kidneys.
pH = 6.1 + log [HCO₃⁻] / (0.03 × PCO₂).

title: List the buffer systems and their importance.
subject: subj:biochem

body.front: List the buffer systems and their importance.
body.back: Extracellular: bicarbonate (main), proteinate (low), phosphate (low, urine). Intracellular: haemoglobin (high), proteins, bone phosphates and carbamates.

title: How does the kidney handle acid?
subject: subj:biochem

body.front: How does the kidney handle acid?
body.back: Reabsorbs filtered HCO₃⁻ (excretes above 28 mmol/L); excretes H⁺ free (urine pH ≥ 4.4) and bound (1/3 titratable, 2/3 NH₄⁺), regenerating one HCO₃⁻ per H⁺.
Arterial (radial, femoral) or capillary in newborns; heparinised syringe; sealed, anaerobic; on ice; analysed within 1 h; note temperature.
pH 7.37-7.43; PaCO₂ 37-43 mmHg; PaO₂ 75-100 mmHg; HCO₃⁻ 22-26 mmol/L; SaO₂ 95-99%; anion gap 12 ± 2; lactate 1-2 mmol/L.
Metabolic acidosis: HCO₃⁻↓, PaCO₂↓. Respiratory acidosis: PaCO₂↑, HCO₃⁻↑. Metabolic alkalosis: HCO₃⁻↑, PaCO₂↑. Respiratory alkalosis: PaCO₂↓, HCO₃⁻↓.

title: Name the catecholamines and their roles.
subject: subj:biochem

body.front: Name the catecholamines and their roles.
body.back: Adrenaline (80 percent of adult secretion), noradrenaline and dopamine. They drive the immediate stress response, meet needs such as exercise, and keep blood pressure and glucose stable, protecting vital functions.

title: Why is the adrenal medulla a modified sympathetic ganglion?
subject: subj:biochem

body.front: Why is the adrenal medulla a modified sympathetic ganglion?
body.back: Embryology: from the neural crest, like sympathetic ganglia. Histology: chromaffin cells in clusters around capillaries. Neurophysiology: catecholamines are also neurotransmitters of nerve cells.
Phenylalanine (phenylalanine hydroxylase) to tyrosine; tyrosine hydroxylase to dopa, the feedback step; decarboxylase to dopamine; dopamine beta-hydroxylase to noradrenaline; PNMT to adrenaline.

Stimulated by the sympathetic system via splanchnic nerves: reflex (low BP, hypoxia, hypercapnia), central (hypoglycaemia, hypothermia), intercentral (pain, emotion, stress, exercise). Hormones: ACTH (dopa, noradrenaline) and cortisol (adrenaline, noradrenaline). Feedback on CNS centres, carotids and tyrosine hydroxylase.

Alpha receptors outnumber beta, but beta have higher affinity for adrenaline. Beta-1: heart rate and force, lipolysis. Beta-2: renin, hepatic glycogenolysis, smooth muscle relaxation. Alpha-1: vasoconstriction, sphincter contraction. Alpha-2: presynaptic inhibition of noradrenaline release.

title: What do catecholamines do to organs?
subject: subj:biochem

body.front: What do catecholamines do to organs?
body.back: Heart: positive chronotropic and inotropic, more venous return; vasodilation in muscle and coronaries, vasoconstriction in gut, kidney, skin; higher output, BP and oxygen use. Gut: less motility. Uterus: beta-2 relaxes (tocolysis), alpha contracts. Bronchi: dilation. Eye: mydriasis. Bladder wall relaxes, sphincter contracts. Muscle: tone up, fatigue delayed. Glands inhibited except sweat.

title: Give the metabolic actions of catecholamines.
subject: subj:biochem

body.front: Give the metabolic actions of catecholamines.
body.back: Mainly via beta receptors: muscle glycogenolysis and inhibition of insulin (mild hyperglycaemia), lipolysis, hyperkalaemia, thermogenesis with cutaneous vasoconstriction.

title: How are catecholamines inactivated and eliminated?
subject: subj:biochem

body.front: How are catecholamines inactivated and eliminated?
body.back: Uptake into nerve endings and storage. Chemical: COMT (70 percent) methylates circulating catecholamines to metanephrine and normetanephrine; MAO (20 percent) deaminates noradrenaline in nerve endings. After hepatic conjugation, urine contains VMA 80 percent (2 to 4 mg/day), metanephrines 10 to 15 percent, free catecholamines 5 percent, little MHPG.

Pheochromocytoma: 90 percent benign, 90 percent adrenal, adults 20 to 50, hypertension (70 percent permanent, 30 percent in fits), excess catecholamines and metanephrines; test plasma metanephrines. Neuroblastoma: malignant, early childhood, adrenal, abdominal or thoracic, non-specific signs, lacks PNMT so dopamine accumulates; test 24-hour urinary dopamine and VMA, plasma NSE.

title: What do calcium and phosphorus do?
subject: subj:biochem

body.front: What do calcium and phosphorus do?
body.back: Both mineralise the skeleton. Calcium: neuromuscular excitability, enzymes, membrane transport, hormone action, clotting. Phosphorus: activating molecules (sugar phosphates), ATP, enzyme regulation, phospholipids and nucleic acids, acid-base buffering.
Three organs (bone, intestine, kidney) and three hormones (PTH, calcitonin, vitamin D).

Needs 800 to 1000 mg/day (1.2 g in growth, pregnancy, lactation, menopause). 1 kg, 99 percent in bone. Serum: 45 percent ionised, 5 percent complexed, 50 percent protein-bound (80 percent to albumin). Absorbed in the duodenum (active calcitriol-dependent, then passive over 600 mg/day). Eliminated in stool and urine; 95 percent of filtered calcium reabsorbed.

Needs 1 g/day (1.2 to 1.4 g in pregnancy). 600 g: 85 percent bone, 14 percent intracellular, 1 percent extracellular. Absorbed in jejunum and ileum (active calcitriol-dependent, passive). Renal: 90 percent of ultrafilterable phosphate reabsorbed proximally, competing with glucose.

PTH (parathyroid, 84 aa, N-terminal active): mobilises bone Ca, raises gut and renal Ca, lowers phosphate: hypercalcaemic, hypophosphataemic. Calcitonin (thyroid C cells): fixes Ca and P on bone, lowers renal reabsorption: lowers both. Calcitriol: raises gut and renal absorption of both, bone turnover: raises both.
Oestrogens raise calcium absorption and mineralisation; thyroid hormones raise absorption and turnover; cortisol lowers mineralisation and absorption.

Calcium: fasting morning, short tourniquet (stasis raises protein and calcium), no EDTA, citrate or oxalate; 85 to 105 mg/L (2.25 to 2.60 mmol/L); correct for albumin. 24-h calciuria in plastic bottles. Phosphate: fasting; adult 30 to 40, child 40 to 60 mg/L. PTH (hypercalcaemia) and vitamin D assays.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biochem

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Bone. Stores 99% of body calcium and 85% of phosphorus.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biochem

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Calcitonin. From thyroid parafollicular cells; lowers calcium and phosphate, no direct gut action.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biochem

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Intestine. Calcium absorbed mainly in the duodenum; phosphorus in the jejunum and ileum.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biochem

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Kidney. Reabsorbs 95% of filtered calcium and 90% of filtered phosphate.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biochem

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Parathyroid hormone. 84 amino acids; N-terminal fragment active; raises calcium and lowers phosphate.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biochem

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Calcitriol. 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol, the most active vitamin D metabolite; raises calcium and phosphate.

title: Roles of calcium and phosphorus beyond bone?
subject: subj:biochem

body.front: Roles of calcium and phosphorus beyond bone?
body.back: Ca: neuromuscular excitability, enzymes, membrane transport, hormone action, clotting. P: sugar-phosphates, ATP, enzyme regulation, phospholipids and nucleic acids, acid-base buffer.
50% diffusible (45% ionised, 5% complexed), 50% protein-bound (80% on albumin).
Duodenum; active, calcitriol-dependent, saturable when intake is low; passive gradient-driven above about 600 mg/day.
About 600 g: 85% bone, 14% intracellular, 1% extracellular; inorganic mostly ultrafilterable (HPO4²⁻ 80%, H2PO4⁻ 20%).
PTH: Ca↑ P↓ (bone, gut, kidney). Calcitonin: Ca↓ P↓ (bone fixation, less renal reabsorption). Calcitriol: Ca↑ P↑ (gut absorption, renal reabsorption, bone turnover).
Morning fasting sample, short gentle tourniquet, no EDTA, citrate or oxalate; 24-h urine in a plastic or decalcified glass bottle.

title: How do you correct calcium for albumin?
subject: subj:biochem

body.front: How do you correct calcium for albumin?
body.back: Corrected Ca (mmol/L) = measured Ca + (40 - albumin g/L)/40.
Two public health problems: acute coronary syndrome (troponins) and chronic heart failure (BNP, NT-proBNP), plus prognostic markers of coronary risk (ultrasensitive CRP).
Myoglobin, CPK, CK-MB, AST and LDH: not specific, no longer routine.
Structural proteins regulating myocyte contraction, with three subunits: T (cardiac isoform cTnT), I (cardiac isoform cTnI) and C (common to all striated muscle, no cardiology use).
Rises 2 hours after pain with high-sensitivity assays, 4 hours with conventional ones; peaks around 14 hours; cTnI stays up 75 to 140 hours, cTnT over ten days, allowing follow-up.
Non-ischaemic myocardial injury (myocarditis, drug toxicity, chemotherapy) and other heart diseases (acute ventricular failure, pericarditis). Assays are not standardised: use one lab.

Cleavage products of proBNP from cardiomyocytes; diuretic, natriuretic and vasodilator. Raised in heart failure and in pulmonary or renal failure, cirrhosis and endocrine disease. Higher with age and in women, lower with high BMI. Always use the same peptide in the same lab; NT-proBNP is practical but distorted in renal failure.

CRP: liver acute phase protein driven by IL-6, promoting phagocyte adhesion and complement. Rises at 6 to 7 h, peaks at 48 to 72 h, normal under 6 mg/L by one week. A persistent low level (under 10 mg/L) signals chronic low-grade inflammation and cardiovascular risk, measured by the ultrasensitive assay (0.01 to tens of mg/L).
Blood tests are non-invasive compared with biopsy; they separate cellular from biliary damage, grade it, orient the diagnosis together, and are sensitive but not specific.

title: Give the liver's anatomy and blood supply.
subject: subj:biochem

body.front: Give the liver's anatomy and blood supply.
body.back: 1.5 kg, right subdiaphragmatic; about 1500 mL/min, 75 percent portal vein and 25 percent hepatic artery; drained by the hepatic veins to the IVC. Functional unit: the lobule. Bile flows from canaliculi to intrahepatic ducts, hepatic ducts, common hepatic duct, joined by the cystic duct as the common bile duct, meeting the pancreatic duct at the ampulla of Vater within the sphincter of Oddi.

A membrane glycoprotein of hepatic origin, 100 times more concentrated in bile. Sample fasting, avoid haemolysis. Normal under 50 IU/L men, 30 women; 7 to 8 times higher in neonates. Isolated rise: chronic alcoholism; also phenobarbital, paracetamol. Most sensitive hepatobiliary indicator; rises with ALP in cholestasis; also in pancreatic disease, diabetes, heart and kidney failure.

Free (unconjugated, fat-soluble, neurotoxic), conjugated (direct) and total. Protect from light. Total 3.4 to 17.1 µmol/L, conjugated 0 to 3.4. Jaundice in the conjunctiva above 30, skin above 50 µmol/L. Conjugated jaundice: bile duct obstruction, hepatocyte canalicular dysfunction, cirrhosis, hepatitis, neoplasia, congenital. Neonatal conjugated jaundice is rare but severe: neonatal hepatitis, biliary atresia.

Ammonium: 98 percent as NH4+, from protein breakdown and gut bacteria, removed only by the liver via the urea cycle; normal 0.3 to 0.7 mg/L; high in severe liver failure or urea cycle defects. Albumin: made only by the liver, 35 to 50 g/L, oncotic pressure and transport. Clotting: prothrombin time lengthens in liver failure and cholestasis; 3 seconds longer means bleeding risk; factors II, V, VII, X, XI.

Alpha-fetoprotein: main fetal protein, rises in hepatocellular carcinoma; screen cirrhosis and chronic hepatitis. Alpha1-antitrypsin deficiency: hereditary, leads to cirrhosis. Ceruloplasmin: copper transport, acute phase protein; collapses in Wilson's disease and liver failure.

Intermediate metabolism (carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, urea cycle), vitamins, iron storage as ferritin; synthesis of albumin, transport proteins and clotting factors; detoxification of drugs, alcohol and free bilirubin; synthesis and excretion of bile, its specific function (about 1 L/day).

Free bilirubin from old red cells is toxic to the brain; the liver conjugates it with glucuronic acid. Conjugated bilirubin goes in bile to the gut, becomes stercobilinogen in stool; a little is reabsorbed into the enterohepatic cycle or excreted in urine as urobilinogen.

Iso-osmotic, greenish yellow, pH 7.6 to 8.6; bile acids, bilirubin, cholesterol, phospholipids, water and electrolytes. It neutralises gastric acid with bicarbonate and forms micelles for fat digestion. Released when CCK contracts the gallbladder and the sphincter of Oddi opens.

title: Name the three liver syndromes and their markers.
subject: subj:biochem

body.front: Name the three liver syndromes and their markers.
body.back: Cytolysis: AST, ALT, LDH. Cholestasis: ALP, GGT, bilirubin. Hepatocellular insufficiency: ammonium, albumin, clotting factors. Specific markers: alpha-fetoprotein, alpha1-antitrypsin, ceruloplasmin.

ALT is more liver-specific; AST is also in heart and muscle. Avoid haemolysis (red cells hold 20 times more AST). Normal under 45 IU/L men, 35 women. Exercise, age and weight raise AST; alcohol and some drugs raise both. Very high in acute hepatitis, moderate in chronic disease; AST alone rises in infarction and muscle damage.
A cytoplasmic enzyme in heart, red cells, kidney, muscle and liver, so not liver-specific. Five isoenzymes: LDH5 liver, LDH1 heart, LDH2 red cells. Adult range 190 to 430 IU/L.

Reduced or stopped bile flow into the gut, from extrahepatic (stones, bile duct or pancreatic head cancer) or intrahepatic (hepatitis, cirrhosis, metastases) causes. In the gut: steatorrhoea, ADEK malabsorption with bleeding, pale stools. In blood: bile acids (pruritus), conjugated bilirubin (jaundice), cholesterol (doubles), ALP and GGT.

A membrane enzyme mainly of liver and bone. Higher in children (bone up to 90 percent) and in pregnancy from week 20; higher in men. Raised in cholestasis, bone disease (fracture healing, osteitis) and some cancers.

title: What is insulin and what does it do?
subject: subj:biochem

body.front: What is insulin and what does it do?
body.back: A peptide hormone from the beta cells of the islets of Langerhans, the only hypoglycaemic hormone, regulating glucose, fatty acids and ketone bodies. Secreted according to nutrition and activity; glucose is stored in muscle, fat and liver. It also affects growth; its absence is fatal within months.

Two chains: A (21 amino acids) and B (30), with two interchain and one intrachain disulphide bridges. Gene on chromosome 11p. Preproinsulin becomes proinsulin (A-B-C), stored in granules; on stimulation a proteinase cleaves off the C-peptide, releasing insulin and C-peptide.

Glucose enters the beta cell and raises ATP, closing K+ channels; the membrane depolarises, opening voltage-gated calcium channels; calcium entry drives exocytosis. Released insulin acts back on its own receptor to activate its gene, restoring reserves.
Activates glycogenesis and glycolysis in liver and muscle, and the pentose phosphate pathway in liver. Inhibits gluconeogenesis, glycogenolysis and glucose release from the liver.

title: Give insulin's lipid, protein and sodium effects.
subject: subj:biochem

body.front: Give insulin's lipid, protein and sodium effects.
body.back: Lipid: fatty acid entry and triglyceride synthesis in adipocytes, glucose entry and conversion to acetyl-CoA; inhibits lipolysis. Protein: amino acid uptake and anabolism; inhibits catabolism and gluconeogenesis. Sodium: stimulates glucose-sodium cotransport.
Activates lipogenesis (fatty acid synthetase) and glycolysis (glucokinase, pyruvate kinase); represses gluconeogenesis.

title: How is diabetes diagnosed and monitored?
subject: subj:biochem

body.front: How is diabetes diagnosed and monitored?
body.back: Diagnosis: fasting glucose, HbA1c (HPLC), glycosuria and ketonuria, oral glucose tolerance test for prediabetes. Monitoring: fasting and postprandial glucose monthly, HbA1c every 2 to 3 months, fructosamine every 15 days if haemoglobinopathy, urine strips, lipid profile, microalbuminuria, creatinine and urea.

About 4 g. Heme (ferrous) iron: 60 percent haemoglobin, 5 percent myoglobin, traces in enzymes. Non-heme (ferric) iron: 35 percent reserves (ferritin, haemosiderin), small plasma fraction on transferrin.

Macrophages destroy old red cells; iron is stored or carried by transferrin back to marrow for erythropoiesis or to the liver for storage. Losses: urine, gut and skin desquamation, appendages, menstruation, pregnancy.

Needs: men 1 mg, women 2 mg, pregnancy 3 then 10 mg/day, more in early childhood and adolescence. About 10 percent absorbed in the duodenum and jejunum, favoured by vitamin C in an acid medium; animal iron better absorbed; absorption rises with bleeding or haemolysis and falls with overload.

Hepatic glycoprotein binding two ferric atoms, one-third saturated; synthesis rises when stores fall. Albumin or lactoferrin carry iron when it is saturated. Erythroblasts are richest in transferrin receptors; the soluble receptor reflects marrow activity.

Ferritin: available reserve in macrophages (mobilised first) and hepatocytes; plasma ferritin mirrors stores. Haemosiderin: stable reserve from lysosomal digestion of ferritin, released slowly, shown by Perls' stain.

Serum iron: men 10 to 30, women 8 to 28 µmol/L (fasting, no iron therapy for a week, no haemolysis). Transferrin 2.4 to 3.8 g/L. TIBC = transferrin x 25 (60 to 95 µmol/L). Saturation = iron / TIBC x 100 (men 20 to 40, women 15 to 35 percent). Ferritin: men 30 to 300, women 20 to 200 µg/L.

Causes: chronic bleeding (digestive in the elderly, genital in women), high demand (pregnancy, breastfeeding, prematurity, blood donation, dialysis), low intake or absorption (IBD, gastrectomy). Three phases: latent, proven, anaemia. Anaemia: Hb under 120 (women) or 130 g/L (men), MCV under 80 fL, hypochromic. Ferritin under 30 µg/L is diagnostic; saturation under 16 percent only late.

Primary haemochromatosis: autosomal recessive, usually HFE mutation lowering hepcidin, with high saturation and non-transferrin-bound iron taken up by liver, heart and pancreas; melanoderma, cirrhosis, diabetes, hypogonadism, heart and joint disease. Secondary: haemolytic anaemias, transfusions, dialysis supplementation, liver disease, atransferrinaemia. Screening: saturation over 45 percent with ferritin over 200 (women) or 300 µg/L (men); HFE testing confirms.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biochem

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Intestinal absorption. Duodenum and upper jejunum; about 10% of dietary iron; helped by vitamin C and acid.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biochem

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Hepcidin. Liver hormone that blocks iron exit from enterocytes and macrophages when iron is high.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biochem

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Macrophage recycling. Macrophages destroy old red cells and release their iron back to transferrin.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biochem

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Bone marrow. Erythroblasts take up iron through transferrin receptors, the richest cells in them.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biochem

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Haemoglobin iron. About 2.4 g, 60% of the 4 g body iron.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biochem

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Iron stores. Ferritin (readily mobilised) and haemosiderin (slow), in liver, spleen and marrow.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biochem

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Transferrin. Liver glycoprotein binding two ferric iron atoms; normally about one-third saturated.
About 4 g: haemoglobin 60% (2.4 g), myoglobin 5%, enzymes traces (haem Fe²⁺); stores 35% (ferritin, haemosiderin) and transferrin-bound plasma iron 0.05 g (non-haem Fe³⁺).
Macrophages destroy old red cells; iron is stored or carried by transferrin to the marrow for new erythroblasts; small losses in urine, desquamation, menstruation, pregnancy.
1 mg/day men, 2 women, 3 then 10 in pregnancy; about 10% absorbed in the duodenum/upper jejunum; vitamin C and acid help; haem iron absorbed best.
Ferritin: readily mobilised store; plasma ferritin reflects stores. Haemosiderin: stable, slow release, lysosomal digestion of ferritin, Perls positive.
TS (%) = plasma iron (µmol/L) / [25 × transferrin (g/L)] × 100; normal men 20-40%, women 15-35%.
Losses (digestive bleeding, menstruation, pregnancy, lactation, prematurity, donation, dialysis) or poor intake/absorption (infants, elderly, IBD, gastrectomy, resection).

title: WHO criteria for iron deficiency anaemia?
subject: subj:biochem

body.front: WHO criteria for iron deficiency anaemia?
body.back: Hb < 120 g/L (women) or < 130 g/L (men), microcytic (MCV < 80 fL), hypochromic.
Autosomal recessive, mostly HFE mutation lowering hepcidin; high iron, low transferrin, TS > 45%, ferritin high late; liver, heart, pancreas overload.

Hyperlipoproteinaemias are common and damage arteries, making them major cardiovascular risk factors. Profiles are done routinely, for clinical signs (obesity, hypertension, sedentary life) and for treatment follow-up.

An apolar core of triglycerides and cholesterol esters, surrounded by phospholipids, free cholesterol and apoproteins. Apoproteins keep the complex soluble and recognise receptors or activate enzymes (Apo AI activates LCAT). Classes A, B, C, D, E.

Triglycerides: glycerol + 3 fatty acids, from food or synthesis from sugars and alcohol; energy reserve. Cholesterol: one third food, two thirds liver; membranes, steroids, bile acids; eliminated in bile with an enterohepatic cycle. Phospholipids: hydrophilic head, two fatty acid tails; membranes.
Chylomicrons: most TG, largest, lightest, Apo B48. VLDL: TG-rich, Apo B100 and C. LDL: rich in cholesterol esters, Apo B100. HDL: rich in phospholipids, densest, Apo A and C.

Dietary TG are digested, absorbed and reassembled into chylomicrons in enterocytes, passing into lymph and blood. The liver makes VLDL from endogenous TG. Endothelial LPL degrades their TG: chylomicrons become remnants cleared by liver B/E receptors; VLDL become IDL then LDL via hepatic lipase. LDL delivers cholesterol to liver and tissues; excess is picked up by HDL, esterified by LCAT and returned to the liver.

title: What does a lipid profile include?
subject: subj:biochem

body.front: What does a lipid profile include?
body.back: Serum appearance, triglycerides, total cholesterol, HDL, calculated or measured LDL; apo AI and B as a complement. Sample after 12-hour fast, 15 min rest, away from acute illness (3 to 4 months after an MI), dry or heparin tube, no haemolysis.

title: Give the reference values and formulas.
subject: subj:biochem

body.front: Give the reference values and formulas.
body.back: TG 0.5 to 1.5 g/L; TC 1.5 to 2 g/L; HDL 0.35 to 0.65 g/L; TC/HDL under 4.9 (men), 4.2 (women). Friedewald LDL = TC − HDL − TG/5 (g/L) if TG under 3.5 g/L; otherwise measure or use Planella. Apo B 0.6 to 1.4 g/L; apo AI over 1.1 g/L; high B/AI ratio = atherogenic.

High cholesterol and/or TG, or high LDL and low HDL, promoting atherosclerosis. Hyperlipoproteinaemia (about 4 percent of adults over 30) is primary (genetic) or secondary (disease, drugs). Hypocholesterolaemia: TC under 1.3 g/L (hereditary or hyperthyroidism, liver disease). Fredrickson classification: type I = excess chylomicrons.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biochem

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Chylomicrons. Made by enterocytes from dietary lipids after a meal; the largest and richest in triglycerides.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biochem

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: HDL. Apo AI activates LCAT, which esterifies free cholesterol; anti-atherogenic.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biochem

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: IDL to LDL. IDL is converted to LDL by hepatic triglyceride lipase.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biochem

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: LDL. Rich in cholesterol esters and apo B100; delivers cholesterol to tissues; atherogenic.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biochem

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: VLDL. Made by the liver from endogenous triglycerides.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biochem

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Lipoprotein lipase. Endothelial enzyme that hydrolyses triglycerides of chylomicrons and VLDL.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biochem

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Chylomicron remnants. Taken up by hepatic B/E receptors and degraded.
Apolar core of triglycerides and cholesterol esters; amphipathic shell of phospholipids, free cholesterol and apoproteins.
Structural (solubilise and transport the complex) and metabolic (bind receptors, activate enzymes such as apo AI activating LCAT).
Chylomicrons: most TG, apo B48, largest. VLDL: hepatic TG, B100. LDL: cholesterol esters, B100. HDL: phospholipids, apo A and C, densest.
Dietary TG → monoglycerides and FA → bile acid micelles → enterocyte chylomicrons → lymph → blood → LPL → remnants cleared by the liver.
Liver VLDL → LPL → IDL → hepatic lipase → LDL → LDL receptors in liver and tissues.

title: Sampling rules for a lipid profile?
subject: subj:biochem

body.front: Sampling rules for a lipid profile?
body.back: 12 h fast, 15 min rest, away from acute illness (3-4 months after MI), dry or heparin tube, no haemolysis.
TG 0.5-1.5 g/L; TC 1.50-2 g/L; HDL 0.35-0.65 g/L; TC/HDL < 4.9 men, < 4.2 women; apo B 0.6-1.40 g/L; apo AI > 1.10 g/L.
LDL = TC - HDL - TG/5 (g/L) or TG/2.2 (mmol/L); only if TG < 3.5 g/L (4 mmol/L).

title: Why does the preanalytical phase matter?
subject: subj:biochem

body.front: Why does the preanalytical phase matter?
body.back: It includes every step before the analysis, often outside the lab, and 68 percent of errors in results come from it, causing extra costs and risks for patients.

title: Name the three phases of analysis.
subject: subj:biochem

body.front: Name the three phases of analysis.
body.back: Preanalytical: steps before the assay. Analytical: the dosage, the heart of the biologist's job, governed by the mandatory GBEA. Postanalytical: results and interpretation.
Upright tubes; analyse within 2 hours, otherwise glucose falls and potassium and transaminases rise. Store at 4 to 8°C if delayed. Protect bilirubin samples from light.

Causes: tight or long tourniquet, syringe turbulence (prefer vacuum), agitation, anaemia, stress, poor veins, long transport. Consequences: false potassium and enzyme results, repeat sampling, delayed care, unnecessary tests, slower lab work.
The prescription (doctor), patient preparation, the equipment and the sampling procedure (nurse), and the sample itself (transport and storage).

title: What clinical information should the prescription give?
subject: subj:biochem

body.front: What clinical information should the prescription give?
body.back: Time of sampling (cortisol, thyroid hormones, adrenaline vary daily), sex (testosterone), age (ALP higher in children from bone growth) and pregnancy (ALP up; proteins, iron and ferritin down).

title: How is blood drawn in a patient on an infusion?
subject: subj:biochem

body.front: How is blood drawn in a patient on an infusion?
body.back: Not from the infused vein; use the opposite arm. Otherwise wait 2 minutes after stopping, sample below the site, discard a first tube, and state the infusion and its type on the request.

Rest 15 minutes in the same position (posture changes proteins and calcium); 12 hours of rest after exercise (CK can quadruple); fast at least 8 hours and sample at 7 to 9 a.m. (lipids can rise 21 percent, serum turns opalescent); avoid stress (prolactin, adrenaline, cortisol).
A conformity marking (CE or FDA), the standard EN/MN 14820 for single-use equipment, and the conditions of use on the leaflet, such as the expiry date.

title: How should the tourniquet be used?
subject: subj:biochem

body.front: How should the tourniquet be used?
body.back: Only if needed: 7 to 10 cm above the site, not too tight, released within 1 minute; unnecessary if veins are visible or palpable. Poor use raises values up to 10 percent. Avoid it for lactate, ammonium, albumin and calcium.

Respect the order of tubes to avoid additive carry-over; never transfer blood; respect filling volume (citrate 1:4); mix gently 5 to 10 times within 2 minutes. Separator gel tubes isolate serum or plasma from cells, stopping glucose use and potassium leak, and protect during transport.

Label tubes immediately after sampling with identity and number, and check the sample matches the request. Identity errors lead to rejection. Non-conformities cost about 25 percent of the sampling budget and must be managed under the GBEA and ISO 15189.
Regulates water-electrolyte and acid-base balance, eliminates toxins, and makes renin, erythropoietin and active vitamin D.

A muscle creatine waste product reflecting muscle mass and GFR, independent of diet and hydration. Sample in the morning, avoid haemolysis and bilirubin, moderate fasting. Men 9 to 12, women 6 to 11, children 3 to 8 mg/L.

Clearance = U x V / P, the plasma volume cleared per unit time; for a substance neither reabsorbed nor secreted it equals GFR. Creatinine clearance = urinary creatinine / serum creatinine x urine flow, normalised to 1.73 m²: men 130 ± 20, women 110 ± 20 mL/min. Errors come from incomplete collection; MDRD formulas avoid this.

title: Stage chronic renal failure by clearance.
subject: subj:biochem

body.front: Stage chronic renal failure by clearance.
body.back: Moderate 50 to 70 mL/min (usually silent); significant 20 to 50; severe 5 to 20 (most biological disorders); under 5: dialysis or transplant.

Osmolar clearance = OsmU x V / OsmP. Concentration test: overnight water fast, morning urine over 800 mOsm/kg. Dilution test: 20 mL/kg water load, one sample near 100 mOsm/kg, 50 percent excreted in 2 hours, 80 percent in 5. Acid-base: bicarbonate reabsorption, titratable acid and ammonia excretion.
Made by the liver from protein-derived ammonia; depends on filtration, fluid intake, dietary protein and catabolism. Sample fasting. 0.15 to 0.45 g/L.

Produced by all cells; more accurate than creatinine, stable from 3 months to 70 years, less affected by sex and muscle. Useful in low muscle mass, early acute renal failure and tubulopathies. Costly, second-line; corticosteroids raise it. 0.5 to 1 mg/L.

End product of purines, varying with diet, age and time of day; rises in renal failure, not always with urea and creatinine. Sample fasting after 3 purine-free days; avoid grey (fluoride-oxalate) tubes. Men 30 to 70, women 20 to 60, children 10 to 35 mg/L.

title: What does the plasma ionogram show?
subject: subj:biochem

body.front: What does the plasma ionogram show?
body.back: Sodium (osmolality), potassium (hyperkalaemia in acute renal failure, life-threatening above 6.5 mmol/L), bicarbonate (acidosis in chronic failure), osmolality [(Na + K) x 2] + urea + glucose = 290 ± 5.

title: What calcium-phosphate changes occur in chronic renal failure?
subject: subj:biochem

body.front: What calcium-phosphate changes occur in chronic renal failure?
body.back: Calcium falls, phosphate and PTH rise: renal osteodystrophy with osteomalacia and secondary hyperparathyroidism, because the kidney can no longer activate vitamin D.
Normal 0.75 to 2 L/day. Polyuria over 2.5 L (renal failure, diabetes insipidus). Oliguria under 0.6 L. Anuria under 0.1 L (acute renal failure). A normal volume does not mean normal function.

Screen with strips (qualitative), confirm in 24-hour urine. Physiological 50 to 150 mg/24 h; functional (orthostatism, effort, hypertension) moderate and intermittent; pathological over 150 mg/24 h and permanent. Microalbuminuria 30 to 300 mg/24 h predicts nephropathy, e.g. diabetic.

title: What do other urine tests show?
subject: subj:biochem

body.front: What do other urine tests show?
body.back: Natriuresis and kaliuresis (Na/K over 1); urinary creatinine 1 to 2 g/24 h for clearance; urinary urea and uric acid (intake, catabolism, concentrating power); urinary calcium and phosphate (stones, secondary hyperparathyroidism).

Separation of serum proteins in an electric field. At pH 8.2 to 8.6 all proteins are anions and migrate towards the anode, separating by size, charge and support porosity. It orients diagnosis, grades severity and follows treatment.
Use serum (dry or clot-activator tube), never plasma, whose fibrinogen adds a band. Avoid haemolysis, whose haemoglobin splits alpha-2. Store at 4°C up to a week.

Agarose gel: semi-automated, 0.1 mL serum, batches of patients, amidoschwartz stain, densitometer reading, 5 bands, about 90 minutes. Capillary zone electrophoresis: fully automated, fast, each patient run independently, same-day results.

title: Name the fractions and their contents.
subject: subj:biochem

body.front: Name the fractions and their contents.
body.back: Albumin: transport, pH buffer, oncotic pressure. Alpha-1 and alpha-2: inflammatory proteins. Beta: includes complement C3. Gamma: immunoglobulins. Normal A/G 1.2 to 1.8.
Albumin falls in pregnancy and old age. Alpha globulins rise in pregnancy, fall in old age. Beta rises in pregnancy and at 40 to 70. Gamma is low in infants and the elderly (hence colostrum).

A dye bubble gives a false peak; CRP over 100 to 150 mg/L gives a gamma peak (should vanish with inflammation, otherwise think of malignancy); haemolysis splits alpha-2; fibrinogen from plasma gives a gamma-region band.

Albumin: bisalbuminaemia; low in malnutrition, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome, inflammation. Alpha-1: low in alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency; high in inflammation. Alpha-2: low in haemolysis; high in inflammation and nephrotic syndrome. Beta: low with C3 consumption; beta-gamma block in cirrhosis. Gamma: low in infants and immunodeficiency; polyclonal (dome) in infection; monoclonal (narrow) in myeloma, lymphoma, benign gammopathy.

High blood protein, unexplained high ESR, recurrent bacterial infections, bone pain or hypercalcaemia (myeloma), suspected inflammation or cirrhosis. It orients rather than confirms; immunofixation types a monoclonal Ig.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biochem

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Alpha-1 globulins. Inflammatory proteins; low in alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biochem

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Alpha-2 globulins. Rise in inflammation and nephrotic syndrome (alpha-2 macroglobulin); fall in haemolysis.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biochem

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Albumin. Most abundant protein, most intense band, migrates furthest toward the anode.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biochem

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Beta globulins. Fall when complement C3 is consumed; merge with gamma in cirrhosis.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biochem

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Beta-gamma block. Polyclonal IgA fills the gap between beta and gamma in alcoholic cirrhosis.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biochem

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Gamma globulins. Immunoglobulins made by lymphoid tissue; polyclonal dome or monoclonal spike.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biochem

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Inflammatory profile. Alpha-1 and alpha-2 both increase.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biochem

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Monoclonal gammopathy. A narrow-based peak: myeloma, lymphoma or benign; confirmed by immunofixation.
In an alkaline buffer (pH 8.2-8.6) all serum proteins are anions and migrate to the anode; speed depends on size, ionic strength and support porosity; five fractions.
Serum in a dry tube (no anticoagulant: fibrinogen), no haemolysis (haemoglobin), store at 4 °C up to a week if delayed.
Gel: semi-automated, batches of patients, amido black and densitometer, ~90 min. Capillary: fully automated, faster, one patient at a time, same-day result.
Dye bubble artefact, high CRP peak in the gamma zone, haemoglobin (haemolysis, splits α2), fibrinogen (plasma instead of serum).
Low intake (malnutrition), low synthesis (cirrhosis), loss (nephrotic syndrome), increased catabolism (severe inflammation).
Inflammation: α1+α2 up. Nephrotic: albumin down, α2 up. Cirrhosis: beta-gamma block. Myeloma: narrow gamma spike. Immune deficiency: low gamma.

title: Monoclonal gammopathy: causes and next step?
subject: subj:biochem

body.front: Monoclonal gammopathy: causes and next step?
body.back: Malignant (myeloma), associated (lymphoma) or benign (elderly); confirm and type by immunofixation (IgG, IgA, IgM, kappa, lambda).
High serum protein, unexplained high ESR, recurrent bacterial infections, bone pain or hypercalcaemia, suspected inflammation or cirrhosis.

title: Name the four types of steroid hormones.
subject: subj:biochem

body.front: Name the four types of steroid hormones.
body.back: Glucocorticoids (cortisol), mineralocorticoids (aldosterone), androgens (testosterone) and female hormones (oestradiol, progesterone). All derive from cholesterol via pregnenolone; each tissue's enzymes decide which it makes.

Adrenal cortex: glomerular (mineralocorticoids), fascicular (mainly glucocorticoids), reticular (androgens from DHEA). Ovaries: oestrogens in the follicular phase, progesterone from the corpus luteum. Testes: Leydig cells make testosterone (95 percent of the total); Sertoli cells support sperm. Placenta: oestrogens and progesterone.

Adrenal (mainly reticular zone): DHEA, circulating as DHEA sulphate; only 1 percent of testosterone. Gonadal: testosterone from androstenedione from puberty, mainly testes. Androstenedione from adrenal DHEA and gonads leads to testosterone and oestrogens.

Requires androgens: oestradiol from testosterone, oestrone from androstenedione, by aromatase. Ovaries (oestradiol 50 to 70 percent before menopause, protecting bone) and placenta (oestriol). After menopause fat takes over and oestrone is 99 percent; obesity raises breast cancer risk.

Oestrogen, progesterone, cortisol and testosterone rise. First trimester: the corpus luteum, driven by HCG. Second and third: the feto-placental unit; fetal adrenal DHEA is hydroxylated by the fetal liver and converted by the placenta to oestriol; the placenta also makes progesterone.

Stress hormone, highest in the morning: catabolism of carbohydrates, fats and proteins, sodium retention, nerve excitability, bone breakdown, anti-inflammatory. In pregnancy: fetal liver glycogen and lung surfactant; lack in preterm babies causes hyaline membrane disease.

title: Give the roles of aldosterone, oestrogens, progesterone and androgens.
subject: subj:biochem

body.front: Give the roles of aldosterone, oestrogens, progesterone and androgens.
body.back: Aldosterone: distal tubule sodium retention, potassium loss, higher volume and BP (with renin-angiotensin). Oestrogens: metabolism, osteoblasts, water retention, secondary sex traits, uterine excitability; their postpartum fall triggers prolactin. Progesterone: implantation, uterine quieting, anti-oestrogenic, opposes lactogenesis in pregnancy. Androgens: protein anabolism, spermatogenesis, male traits, oestrogen precursors, fetal genital differentiation.

Hypothalamus: CRH and GnRH. Anterior pituitary: ACTH (corticotroph cells) acts on the adrenal cortex (cortisol, aldosterone, adrenal androgens); FSH on gonads (oestrogens); LH on gonads (progesterone). Hormones feed back negatively.

Theca cells make androgens; granulosa cells convert them to oestradiol. After ovulation, luteal cells secrete progesterone, which theca cells can turn into androstenedione and testosterone, and granulosa cells into oestradiol.

C18 oestrogens: E1 oestrone (menopause), E2 oestradiol (active women), E3 oestriol (pregnancy only). C19 androgens: DHEA and DHEA-S (adrenal), androstenedione (adrenal and gonads), testosterone, and DHT (most potent). C21: progesterone, cortisol, aldosterone.
Hydroxylases (add OH), desmolases (cut carbon bonds after hydroxylation), and the dehydrogenase + isomerase pair (remove two hydrogens, shift a double bond).

title: Describe the common stage of synthesis.
subject: subj:biochem

body.front: Describe the common stage of synthesis.
body.back: In mitochondria, a hydroxylase acts on carbons 20 and 22 and cholesterol 20-22 desmolase cuts the chain, giving pregnenolone. The desmolase is the key enzyme, stimulated by ACTH (adrenal) and LH and FSH (gonads). In microsomes, 17-alpha-hydroxylase and 3-beta dehydrogenase-isomerase give 17-OH pregnenolone, progesterone and 17-OH progesterone.

title: How is cortisol made and cleared?
subject: subj:biochem

body.front: How is cortisol made and cleared?
body.back: In the fascicular zone, from 17-OH progesterone by 21-hydroxylase then 11-beta-hydroxylase. About 20 mg/day, inactivated in the liver to cortisone by 11-beta-dehydrogenase.

Inherited 21-hydroxylase deficiency: 17-OH progesterone accumulates and is diverted to DHEA and androgens; cortisol and aldosterone fall. Without cortisol feedback, ACTH rises, the desmolase is overactive and the cortex hypertrophies. At birth: ambiguous genitalia in girls; later: salt-losing dehydration, primary amenorrhoea, early puberty, hirsutism. Steroids before week 6 of amenorrhoea prevent virilisation.

Only in the glomerular zone, via progesterone: 21-hydroxylase gives deoxycorticosterone (weak mineralocorticoid), 11-beta-hydroxylase gives corticosterone, then 18-hydroxylation and dehydrogenation give aldosterone, the main regulator of electrolyte balance.

title: What is the progesterone receptor mutation case?
subject: subj:biochem

body.front: What is the progesterone receptor mutation case?
body.back: A rare genetic gestational hypertension: the mutated aldosterone receptor recognises progesterone, normally an anti-mineralocorticoid, as a potent agonist; pregnancy's high progesterone then causes hypertension.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biochem

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Iodide capture. Follicular cells take up iodide from the blood by active transport; inside it is 30 times more concentrated.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biochem

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Coupling. TPO couples DIT + DIT into T4 and DIT + MIT into T3, still bound to thyroglobulin.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biochem

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Iodination. TPO binds iodine to tyrosines of thyroglobulin: one iodine gives MIT, two give DIT.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biochem

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Release. Thyroglobulin re-enters by endocytosis; lysosomal enzymes free the hormones; deiodinase recycles iodine from MIT and DIT.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biochem

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Iodide oxidation. Thyroid peroxidase (TPO) oxidises iodide to active organic iodine (I2) at the apical pole.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biochem

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Peripheral conversion. Most T3 is made in peripheral tissues from T4 by deiodinase; T3 is 10 times more active.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biochem

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Secretion. Only T3, T4 and reverse T3 are secreted; T4 is about 90%; only T3 and T4 are active.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biochem

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Transport proteins. TBG (from the liver) binds T4 most; TBPA binds mainly T3; albumin is non-specific. Bound hormone is inactive.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biochem

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Thyroglobulin. Made in the ribosomes, processed in the ER and Golgi, then discharged into the colloid.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biochem

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: TSH. Pituitary glycoprotein (common alpha, specific beta chain) that activates every step of synthesis.

title: Where is iodide oxidised, and by what?
subject: subj:biochem

body.front: Where is iodide oxidised, and by what?
body.back: At the apical pole of the thyrocyte, by thyroid peroxidase (TPO), into active organic iodine.
DIT + DIT = T4 (thyroxine); DIT + MIT = T3.

title: Why is T4 used for replacement?
subject: subj:biochem

body.front: Why is T4 used for replacement?
body.back: Half-life 1 week (T3 1 day): once daily, better compliance, converted to T3 in tissues.
Iodine-containing antiarrhythmic: thyroid check before, then every 6 months (tutorial: until 1 year after stopping).

title: Which hormones are secreted into the blood?
subject: subj:biochem

body.front: Which hormones are secreted into the blood?
body.back: T4 (90%), T3 and reverse T3 (inactive). MIT and DIT are not secreted.

title: Which form of thyroid hormone is active?
subject: subj:biochem

body.front: Which form of thyroid hormone is active?
body.back: The free form (FT4, FT3); bound hormone is inactive.
TBG (main, binds T4), TBPA (mainly T3), albumin (non-specific).
In peripheral tissues, from T4, by deiodinase.
Glycoprotein: alpha chain common to TSH, LH, FSH, hCG; specific beta chain.
Conjugation in the liver; deamination/decarboxylation/oxidation (TRIAC, TETRAC); deiodination in the kidney (80%).
Graves: anti-TSH receptor. Hashimoto: anti-thyroglobulin, anti-microsomal, anti-peroxidase.
FT4 makes the positive diagnosis; TSHus locates the problem (central or peripheral).
About 60 percent of body weight (42 L at 70 kg); 50 percent in women, 75 percent in infants, less in the elderly. Muscle 75, bone 22, fat 10 percent. Rapid weight change suggests water gain or loss.
In 2.5 L: drinks 2.2, food 0.7 (as listed), metabolic water 0.3. Out 2.5 L: urine 1.5, insensible losses 0.9, stool 0.1.
Intracellular: 40 to 50 percent of body weight, two thirds of water, 28 L. Extracellular 20 percent: interstitial and lymph 15 percent (12 L, a plasma ultrafiltrate), plasma 5 percent (3 L).

title: Compare the ionic composition of the sectors.
subject: subj:biochem

body.front: Compare the ionic composition of the sectors.
body.back: Plasma: Na+ main cation, Cl- main anion, then HCO3- and proteins. Intracellular: K+ main cation, phosphates then proteins, little Na+ and Cl-. Interstitial: plasma without proteins (Donnan: anions x1.05, cations x0.95). All sectors are electrically neutral; mEq = mmol x valence.

title: How do water and ions move between sectors?
subject: subj:biochem

body.front: How do water and ions move between sectors?
body.back: Across cell membranes: ions by diffusion or active transport (Na+/K+ ATPase); water by osmosis toward the more concentrated side. Across capillaries (Starling): hydrostatic pressure pushes water out at the arterial end, oncotic pressure pulls it back at the venous end.

Extra-renal: shifts between sectors and thirst. Renal: ADH (water reabsorption in collecting ducts), RAAS (renin in hypovolaemia, then aldosterone retains Na+ and water), ANF (diuretic, natriuretic, vasodilator).

title: Give the preanalytical rules for the ionogram.
subject: subj:biochem

body.front: Give the preanalytical rules for the ionogram.
body.back: Avoid haemolysis and delay (false K+); no sodium heparin (false Na+) or EDTA (false K+); hypertriglyceridaemia and hyperprotidaemia give false hyponatraemia. Store treated samples a week at 4°C; 24-h urine without antiseptic.

Na+ 135 to 145 mmol/L, 90 percent extracellular, sets osmotic pressure. Hyponatraemia: renal or digestive sodium loss, excess water, ADH hypersecretion. Hypernatraemia: excess sodium (hypertonic serum), low water intake, water loss (diuretics, hyperglycaemia, fever, sweating, diarrhoea).

K+ 3.5 to 5.5 mmol/L. Hypokalaemia: constipation, cramps, hypotonia, cardiac signs; from vomiting, diarrhoea, hyperaldosteronism, tubulopathy, poor intake. Hyperkalaemia over 5.5, life-threatening over 6.5: K+ infusion, renal failure, cell lysis (burns). Cl- 95 to 108, parallel to Na+, opposite to HCO3-; high in excess intake, tubulopathy, dehydration; low in vomiting and diuretics.

Calculated osmolality = (Na + K) x 2 + urea + glucose = 280 to 300 mOsm/kg; osmolarity 280 to 295 mOsm/L; sodium reflects it. Extracellular dehydration: isotonic loss (vomiting, diarrhoea, heat stroke, renal). Intracellular dehydration: water deficit (intubation, head injury, diabetes insipidus). Extracellular hyperhydration (oedema): renal, heart failure, cirrhosis. Intracellular hyperhydration: low osmolarity from sodium loss or dilution.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biochem

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Intracellular compartment. Two thirds of body water (28 L); potassium and phosphates dominate.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biochem

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Interstitial fluid. About 12 L; plasma ultrafiltrate without proteins (Donnan equilibrium).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biochem

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Cell membrane exchange. Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase expels sodium; water follows osmolality.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biochem

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Plasma. About 3 L; sodium and chloride dominate, with bicarbonate and proteins.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biochem

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Regulation. Thirst, ADH (water), RAAS/aldosterone (sodium and water), ANF (natriuresis).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biochem

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Capillary exchange. Hydrostatic pressure pushes water out at the arterial end; oncotic pressure pulls it back at the venous end.

title: How is body water distributed at 70 kg?
subject: subj:biochem

body.front: How is body water distributed at 70 kg?
body.back: 42 L total: intracellular 28 L (40-50% of weight), interstitial 12 L (15%), plasma 3 L (5%).
In: drinks 2.2 L, food 0.7 L, metabolic water 0.3 L (as given in the lecture). Out: urine 1.5 L, insensible 0.9 L, stool 0.1 L; about 2.5 L each way.

title: Ionic composition of plasma vs cells?
subject: subj:biochem

body.front: Ionic composition of plasma vs cells?
body.back: Plasma: Na⁺ main cation, Cl⁻ main anion, then HCO₃⁻ and proteins. Cells: K⁺ main cation, phosphates main anion, then proteins.
Interstitial fluid lacks proteins, so it has slightly more anions (×1.05) and fewer cations (×0.95) than plasma.

title: List the hormonal regulators of water and sodium.
subject: subj:biochem

body.front: List the hormonal regulators of water and sodium.
body.back: ADH (water only, collecting duct), RAAS/aldosterone (sodium and water), ANF (diuretic, natriuretic, vasodilator); plus thirst.
Haemolysis and delay (false high K⁺), sodium heparin (false Na⁺), EDTA (false K⁺), hypertriglyceridaemia and hyperproteinaemia (false hyponatraemia).
Hypo: sodium loss (renal, digestive), excess water, ADH excess. Hyper: excess sodium, water deficit, water loss (renal, insensible, intestinal).
Extracellular: isotonic loss (vomiting, diarrhoea, heat stroke). Intracellular: water deficit (intubation, head injury, diabetes insipidus). Global: cystic fibrosis, infant gastroenteritis, diabetes.
